meetings.headline: The layoffs-reckoning meeting
meetings.record_note: Live notes from an AI-assisted transcript of the meeting; official district minutes to come. All votes were voice votes ("all in favor, aye"), with no roll call and no audible opposition recorded.

items.title: Developer fee raised to $3.72 per square foot
items.why: The new rate takes effect in January, up from $3.31, and is shared with the high school district, which the district will notify. Matthew Morgan first read the study's recommended $3.59, then corrected himself from the document: $3.72 is the actual total. A speaker warned the roughly 40-cent jump will hurt families building a second home on their property. Passed by voice vote.

items.title: Board commits 3% of spending to a reserve
items.why: About $210,000 into a separate reserve fund (Fund 17), on top of the 17% the state recommends, bringing total reserves to 20%. Morgan called the 3% a goal rather than a yearly amount; projections for the next two years show only about $6,000 of room. The general fund is running $194,000 ahead, with about $50,000 in administrative savings.

items.title: The layoffs' toll on classified staff, relayed to the board
items.why: Staff concerns reached the board secondhand, reported from an earlier meeting with the classified staff union (CSEA) attended by Matthew Morgan and at least one board member. Last summer's layoffs broke trust: wage and hour cuts hit people making rent and feeding families, most staff were rehired but a few were not or came back to fewer hours, and cutting larger positions forced reductions on everyone below them, hitting some longtime staff again in a long, drawn-out process. At the union meeting, every person was described as frustrated or furious, devastated, or feeling undervalued; some said traumatized. Classified staff were called surrogate parents who go nonstop with very little downtime and no prep time, while student behavior problems were described as higher than they have ever been. A board member called the process not at all perfect and its timing unfortunate, and said staff should know how much they are valued; one speaker pledged better communication and a hard look for other cuts, revenue, and grants so that staff are not cut. Ideas raised: time away from students for basic tasks, with support staff rotating to cover each other; board listening sessions two or three times a year whether or not there is a problem; and one-on-ones with Morgan, with a union representative present if staff prefer, with board members as another channel for concerns.

items.title: Admin restructuring plan sketched, $127k in savings
items.why: Morgan proposed more business support from the county office to cover departing business chief Stacey's work, stipends or added hours for Lindsay and Melina, possibly a district secretary for communications, and redesigning his own role. He returns in December for direction once county figures and staff input are in. Stacey is leaving for a bigger district, two new board members will need onboarding, and the December 15 meeting will recognize the departures.

items.title: Bond project list adopted; Measure M leaning toward passage
items.why: The list sets priorities and phases, not specific contracts; a request for architect qualifications comes next. Late votes on the Measure M bond favor passage, and Amanda Jacobs found a USDA grant worth about $57,000.

items.title: Creek fix likely means boulders
items.why: A geotechnical engineer walked the creek and found bedrock pushing water into the bank; placing boulders is the likely fix. Permitting is slow, with a site walk by Pernisky Chatham next. Forestry work takes about a week, with debris burned in spring.

items.title: Conflict-of-interest code updated after 25 years
items.why: Resolution 2627, requested by Sonoma County, is the first update since the code was written: disclosure filing now follows the district's current roles, the trustees, superintendent/principal, and a chief business official replacing the old "business manager" title, with annual updates from now on. Passed by voice vote.

items.title: West County Consortium needs a new host district
items.why: The West County Consortium pools special-education staff (speech-language pathologists, psychologists, nurses, occupational therapists, behavior assistants, and specialized classrooms) for about nine small West County elementary districts, including Harmony. For more than 20 years the West Sonoma County Union High School District has served as its host district (LEA), receiving the funding, employing the roughly 39 staff, and carrying compliance. That district has proposed stepping down as host, calling the arrangement no longer financially or programmatically advantageous for it; the current agreement among districts runs through 2027-28, and an early exit requires another district or agency to take over hosting. About 220 students are served. The board discussion continues.

items.title: Enrollment at 207; classroom and community notes
items.why: Tammy started part-time November 2 and Jeanette full-time November 3. The Shark parent group reported summer music training for teachers, a local author visit for reading week, and the Color Run held in the rain; feedback on the Thinking Math pilot is mixed.

items.title: Facilities master plan adopted; state application authorized
items.why: Three unanimous OPSC items: correcting the district's 2012 filing, submitting the 2026 one, and adopting Resolution 20261030 — the facilities master plan plus authorization to apply to the state's school-construction funding program. This is the pipeline the board has been assembling since September's $17M needs list, now formalized as a state application. In and out in an hour (8:57–10:01 AM), every vote unanimous.

items.title: Two hires approved
items.why: A special-education paraeducator and a custodial/maintenance technician — the October starts flagged at the September meeting.

items.title: November meeting moved
items.why: November 12 shifts to Monday, November 16, 2026 — 7:00 PM via Google Meet per the district calendar.

items.title: Pathways financials on the November agenda
items.why: The board requested a November discussion item: a Pathways financial explanation and how it affects Harmony Union School District.

meetings.headline: The first real bond money moves

items.title: Bond contracts approved — about $83K
items.why: Unanimous consent (Laird/Solter): cargo storage ($34,000), EOC pad ($13,000), perimeter survey ($8,000), septic risers ($12,000), and cistern/garden water overflow ($16,000) — the first Measure M bond contracts actually executed, not just budgeted.

items.title: Field trips (consent)
items.why: Overnight and water-related student trips approved.

items.title: William's Law quarterly reports
items.why: Q4 2025-26 and Q1 2026-27 school-safety reporting approved unanimously — the state's quarterly confirmation the district is current.

items.title: Five minutes flat
items.why: The open session ran 9:16 to 9:21 PM — every vote unanimous, no discussion on the record. The board's real work that night happened in closed session beforehand; the open session was the rapid-fire sign-off.

items.title: Next meeting: November 12
items.why: Confirmed on the record — since moved to November 16 per the October 30 minutes.

items.title: 2025-26 unaudited actuals approved — unanimous
items.why: Convened 8:49 AM, adjourned 8:52 AM — the meeting's one substantive act. The district's closed books for 2025-26 (Gress/Laird, unanimous), headed to the county office. The full report runs about a hundred pages; the headline numbers are on the budget page — including an attendance shortfall worth roughly $160K in state funding.

meetings.headline: The workhorse — nine approvals, every vote unanimous

items.title: Money items
items.why: LCAP revisions, unaudited actuals, the Gann limit (the state's spending cap), and substitute teacher compensation — all approved unanimously.

items.title: Facilities and energy
items.why: PCO Energy Resiliency Project, a PG&E contract, and a new facilities fee schedule — all approved.

items.title: New math pilot
items.why: Innovamat Thinking Math approved for piloting.

items.title: The bond pipeline
items.why: $17M in identified project needs; $1M–$2.5M potentially bond-fundable; committee phases finalized, due January 2027.

items.title: People
items.why: New special-education and custodial hires start in October. Closed session covered union negotiations (CSEA and HUTA), anticipated litigation, and the superintendent's review.

items.title: shARK fundraising
items.why: $11K pledged toward a $20K goal.

items.title: What's coming
items.why: Parcel tax discussions (Koslen), a Town Hall on October 15, and new-board-member training January 14.

items.title: Closed session: two anticipated litigation matters
items.why: Almost the entire hour was legal counsel in closed session. No report out, no votes, no dollars. The public record is essentially "we met with our lawyer."
